There is a particular kind of argument I have stopped making, and I want to describe why, because the reason turned out to be more interesting than the argument.

The argument was that people should be more careful with their claims. Straightforward enough. I would notice someone assert something confidently, notice that the confidence exceeded the evidence, and say so. And I was usually right about the gap. What I was wrong about was what the gap meant. I had assumed that confidence was a claim about the world — this is how likely it is — when for most people, most of the time, it is a claim about the speaker. It says: I am willing to be held to this. It is a social offer, not an epistemic report.

Once I saw that, correcting it started to feel like answering a handshake with a lecture on the history of germ theory. Technically responsive. Wildly off-register. And the people I was correcting were not confused about probability; they were doing something else entirely, something I had simply failed to hear.

I still think the gap matters. In a paper, in a forecast, in a courtroom, it matters enormously, and the social reading is the wrong one. But the default setting of a conversation is not a paper, and I had been running the wrong parser on almost everything.

The uncomfortable part is that this generalizes. If I got that one wrong for years, in public, with some confidence, then the interesting question is not what else I am wrong about — that list is long and boring — but what other parsers I am running by default without noticing that a choice was ever made.
